checkpoints: init: the client POSTs filename, the true byte size, and an optional chunkSize; the server itself computes totalChunks = ceil(size / chunkSize) — never trusting a client-declared chunk count, which would let assembly diverge.
init creates a session {id, filename, size, chunkSize, totalChunks, receivedIndices, finalized} and returns sessionId + totalChunks + chunkSize.

chunk delivery: each PATCH by index carries a raw binary body, and that route must be exempted from the framework's default body parser, since any JSON/text parsing would re-interpret or corrupt the binary data; the index is validated to lie within [0, totalChunks).

chunk delivery is idempotent: writing the file overwrites the same path on disk, and a membership check runs before adding to the received set, so re-sending the same chunk any number of times converges to exactly one file and exactly one entry.

status: it returns the set of received indices and the set of missing indices, so a client that lost connectivity knows exactly what to re-send — resume means sending only the missing pieces, never restarting from zero.

finalize rejects with a missing-chunk count if the session isn't complete; once complete, it assembles strictly in order 0..N-1 regardless of arrival order, computing a checksum during that same merge pass so the file never needs a second read.

the last chunk being naturally smaller whenever size doesn't divide evenly by chunkSize needs no special casing, since each chunk is written with exactly the bytes it received and the merge pass reads each file sequentially in full.

on robustness: the session store is just an interface — in-memory for a demo, a shared TTL'd store (Redis or a DB) for production — without changing the four endpoints' contract; init is rate-limited per client and a periodic cleanup job removes sessions past their TTL, so abandoned sessions can't flood the service or fill up disk.

Core invariant: every upload has a single, durable, authoritative Upload-Offset that the server commits to remembering and the client commits to echoing back correctly — every deployment decision exists only to protect this contract once the system runs on more than one instance.

A disk-local FileStore only works for a single machine: with a load balancer routing round-robin, the next HEAD/PATCH can land on an instance that never saw the file and returns a wrong offset (zero or not-found), sending the client into an endless 409 loop or, worse, corrupting the file by writing at the wrong offset.

Fix: move the datastore to a shared S3-style object store (S3Store/GCSStore) so the offset lives in the object's metadata on shared storage, and every replica reads the exact same value, so any instance answers an offset query truthfully.

A shared store alone does not solve two clients writing at once — e.g. two browser tabs resuming the same upload with the same fingerprint send PATCH nearly simultaneously, both read offset N and both try to write from N, and without serialization one overwrites or inserts in the wrong place.

Fix: a per-upload distributed lock (e.g. Redis SET NX EX) held for exactly the duration of one PATCH, with a request arriving while the lock is held getting 423 Locked instead of being processed in parallel — the off-the-shelf server ships with no such lock, so this layer must be added once running more than one instance — and the protocol's own offset-mismatch mechanism (a PATCH whose Upload-Offset doesn't match the server's stored offset gets 409, requiring the client to re-HEAD and resync before retrying) serves as a second safety net catching whatever race slips past the lock.

An incomplete upload needs a TTL plus a periodic cleanup job removing expired slots, so a resume HEAD sent after the TTL expires gets 404 even though the fingerprint is still sitting in the client's localStorage.

The client-side contract must treat 404 on HEAD as 'the slot is gone' rather than a transient error — clearing the stored fingerprint→uploadUrl mapping and POSTing a brand-new upload — otherwise the client keeps HEADing the dead URL and the resume hangs forever.

Because an upload may resume hours or days later, the auth token attached at POST-creation time is likely expired by the next PATCH; if the middleware only guards POST, every resumed PATCH gets 401 and the upload stalls even though server and client are otherwise healthy — the fix is authenticating every state-mutating request (PATCH and HEAD too) with a currently-valid token, plus a refresh endpoint the client calls before resuming if the old token has expired.
Raising the timeout only masks the symptom; the deeper problem is that a single HTTP request is stateless and atomic — the server either finishes it in one shot or has nothing to show for it.

Intermediaries (load balancers, reverse proxies, sometimes the client's own network stack) enforce their own timeouts regardless of the app server's configured limit, so a 1 GB transfer on a slow or flaky connection can still blow through 60-300 seconds even after 'fixing' the server config.
There is zero resumability: because the whole file lives inside one request, an interruption at byte N leaves the server with nothing usable, forcing the client to restart from byte 0.

The server pays a real resource cost holding a connection (and typically buffering or streaming a body) open for minutes per upload, which does not scale once several large uploads happen concurrently.
Chunked upload fixes this by moving progress out of the HTTP connection and into a session: POST /uploads/init computes totalChunks = ceil(size / chunkSize) and creates a session object server-side.

Each chunk is delivered as its own short PATCH request carrying only a few megabytes, so no single request is ever near the timeout wall and only a small slice of the file occupies memory or a connection at any moment.

GET /uploads/:id/status exposes exactly which chunk indices have been received and which are missing, so a client that drops and reconnects resumes by re-sending only the gaps instead of starting over.

POST /uploads/:id/finalize is the gate: it checks the received count against totalChunks first and rejects the call with a clear 'chunks missing' error if anything is outstanding, only assembling the file and computing its checksum once every chunk has actually landed.

Today's architecture pays for two legs — client-to-server then server-to-S3 — doubling bandwidth and holding one server request thread/connection open per upload for its full duration, turning the app tier into an IO bottleneck at thousands of concurrent uploads; after migrating to presigned direct upload, the client requests a presigned PUT URL and PUTs straight to S3/MinIO, leaving the server to only sign the URL — a sub-millisecond computation with no CPU/RAM cost and no file bytes touching the server at all.
The server must still authenticate the user before signing — only sign a URL for a request that has already passed auth, never sign unconditionally.

The server must still generate the object key itself, server-side, in a monotonically increasing, unguessable, collision-free form (e.g. Date.now()-randomUUID) — never letting the client choose its own key.
The server must choose a short TTL for the signed URL to bound the attack window if it leaks.
The server must keep the upload-signing endpoint (PutObjectCommand) separate from the download-signing endpoint (GetObjectCommand), since these represent two different permission sets.

New failure mode — the orphan object: the client PUTs successfully to storage, but the app crashes or errors before writing that key to the DB, leaving an object that still exists and keeps costing storage with nobody aware of it; the fix is uploading into a temporary prefix like temp/, only copying to the final location and deleting the temp copy once the DB write is confirmed, plus a lifecycle rule that auto-deletes anything left in temp/ after a few hours, or a periodic cron cross-referencing storage keys against the DB to delete orphaned keys.

New failure mode — the bucket needs a CORS rule allowing PUT from the app's origin; without it the browser blocks the request itself before it ever leaves the client, failing silently even though the server signed the URL perfectly correctly.

Because the server no longer sees the bytes to check content-type/size itself, those constraints must move into the signature itself — signing the content-type so a different header at PUT time invalidates the signature (403), and signing a size limit so the client can't upload any size within the TTL; the signed URL itself is the bearer token for all that authority, so it must never be logged and its TTL kept as short as practical.
Disk streaming pipes bytes to disk as they arrive, keeping RAM flat regardless of file size — the right call for large files and high concurrency.

The trade-off of disk streaming is that a file rejected by any post-write validation step is already sitting on disk and must be manually unlink-ed in the failure path, or orphaned files eat disk space.
Memory buffering holds the file as a single buffer, making it easy to validate before deciding where it goes, with a clean handoff to an object-storage SDK and no local disk touch at all.
The trade-off of memory buffering is that its memory cost equals concurrent uploads times file size, so it is only safe with a strict size cap attached.
Non-negotiable in both strategies: a fileSize limit must be enforced mid-stream while the bytes are still arriving, not after everything has already been received.

Decision rule: files larger than a few MB or of unpredictable size go to disk streaming, accepting the unlink obligation on validation failure; small, size-bounded files whose final destination is S3-style storage go to memory buffer plus validate plus forward, the most common pattern in real upload-to-object-storage pipelines.

Both designs solve the same problem — moving upload state out of the fragile HTTP connection into a durable, server-side resource, so a dropped connection loses only the bytes in flight, not the whole upload — they just differ in how much of that is standardized.

The verbs line up almost one-to-one: tus's OPTIONS has no real analogue in a custom API (a bespoke API can simply skip capability discovery), POST is exactly init (creates the upload slot and returns an identifier, no bytes travel), PATCH is exactly chunk delivery, and HEAD is exactly status.

tus tracks one durable byte offset: every PATCH must carry Upload-Offset equal to the server's stored offset, chunks are appended strictly in order, and the server hands back the new offset each time — resuming means reading that single number.

A custom chunk-index scheme tracks a SET of received indices instead, so chunks can arrive out of order or in parallel (which a single offset cannot express), but resuming now means computing the missing-index set rather than reading one field.

tus validates the client's claimed offset against the stored one on every PATCH and answers 409 Conflict the moment they disagree, rejecting a retry that raced an already-committed append rather than silently duplicating bytes, with the client expected to re-HEAD to resync before trying again.

An index-based API has no single durable counter to validate against, so it earns the same idempotency by overwriting on the same index (writing chunk 7 again just replaces chunk 7) plus a duplicate-count guard to catch a client that thinks it never got a response.

Adopting tus buys a standard wire contract — mature clients already exist for browser, iOS, and Android, off-the-shelf servers exist for most backend stacks, and protocol extensions like deferred length and server-side concatenation are already specified — so you are not inventing and documenting your own contract.

Building a custom index API earns its keep when the upload needs a bespoke session lifecycle or internal authorization model a generic tus server can't express, or when the backend language has no mature tus server library worth trusting, and it is not a dead end since its lifecycle can be adapted toward the tus wire contract later if cross-platform clients become a requirement.

A presigned URL functions as a bearer token — whoever holds it is treated as authorized — but that authorization is tightly bounded by scope, time, and signed-parameter integrity, not open-ended like a real credential.
The secret key that signed the URL never leaves the server, so there is no privilege-escalation path at all.
Scope control: each presigned URL is limited to one operation on one key.
Time control: TTL defaults to a short window (e.g. 300 seconds); after expiry MinIO returns 403 "Request has expired," so TTL should be set only as long as the user needs to finish the operation.

Integrity control: every signed parameter (key, bucket, content-type) is immutable — altering any of them breaks the HMAC-SHA256 signature and returns 403; concretely, PutObjectCommand signs a specific content-type so a mismatched Content-Type header is rejected.

Known gap: content-length is not currently part of the signature (ContentLength is never set on the request), so an attacker holding the URL can PUT an arbitrarily large payload to that key for the entire TTL window — declared size must be validated server-side before signing, with a length cap signed alongside.
Operational hygiene: HTTPS only, never log presigned URLs, only sign for an already-authenticated user, and keep the upload-signing endpoint's policy separate from the download-signing endpoint's.
Net conclusion: this mechanism is categorically safer than shipping real credentials to the client, provided TTL discipline and signed-parameter discipline both hold.

Multer enforces `limits.fileSize` by aborting the multipart stream mid-transfer the moment the byte count crosses the configured cap, and it does this while `FileInterceptor` is still parsing the request body — before the route handler ever executes.

Because the abort happens inside the interceptor layer, the route handler's own logic (including any `if (!file)` check written for the wrong-MIME case) never runs for an oversized upload, so a try/catch placed inside the handler cannot intercept this failure.

When the size limit trips, Multer throws its own error class, `MulterError`, with `code = "LIMIT_FILE_SIZE"` — this is not a NestJS `HttpException`, so it carries no built-in mapping to an HTTP status.

NestJS's default exception handling only knows how to translate `HttpException` instances into structured responses; an unrecognized error type like `MulterError` falls through that default handling and surfaces as a generic 500 with a raw stack trace instead of a meaningful status.

The fix is a dedicated exception filter — a class implementing `ExceptionFilter` decorated with `@Catch(MulterError)` — that switches on `exception.code`, mapping `LIMIT_FILE_SIZE` to a 413 Payload Too Large response and other Multer error codes to 400, each with a standardized JSON body.

Registering the filter globally via `app.useGlobalFilters(...)` in `main.ts`, rather than scoping it to one controller with `@UseFilters`, ensures every upload route in the application gets covered by the same mapping instead of only the endpoint being debugged.

Returning 413 instead of 500 changes what the response communicates to the client: 413 signals a client-side problem (the file itself was too large) so the client can show a targeted message and avoid retrying, whereas 500 implies a server fault and exposes internal error detail with no actionable next step.

Fixing this correctly means verifying an over-limit upload now returns 413 with the standardized body while a valid-size upload still returns 201 and a wrong-MIME upload still returns 415 — proving the new filter only intercepts `MulterError` and leaves the controller's own MIME-check path untouched.
Retrying a chunk PATCH after a lost response can deliver the same chunk index more than once, so the handler for that index has to converge to one identical result no matter how many times it runs.

Opening the part file in append mode means a repeated delivery of the same index stacks its bytes onto the previous write, so that chunk's file grows past its real size and the assembled output ends up larger than the source with a mismatched SHA-256.

At the disk-write layer, idempotency means writing a given chunk index any number of times must overwrite the prior content and leave exactly one file of the correct size, not accumulate bytes across deliveries.
Pushing an index onto receivedChunks without first checking whether it is already present lets a retried chunk inflate receivedChunks.length even though no new data actually arrived.

Because finalize decides completeness purely by comparing receivedChunks.length to totalChunks, an inflated count from one duplicated index can make that comparison pass while a different chunk was never actually received.

At the session-bookkeeping layer, idempotency means recording a given index any number of times must count as exactly one entry, so the received count reflects distinct chunks rather than delivery attempts.
Both symptoms — an oversized/corrupted assembled file and a finalize that reports success too early — trace back to the same missing guarantee: writeChunk was never made idempotent per chunk index.

Proving the fix needs three checks: resending the same index and confirming the part-file size and received count stay unchanged, calling finalize while a chunk is genuinely missing and confirming it is rejected, and running a full upload with injected retries and confirming the final SHA-256 still matches the source.

Building a physical filename by concatenating a timestamp with `file.originalname` embeds client-controlled input directly into a filesystem path — a value like `../../../etc/cron.d/evil` walks the write straight out of the intended upload directory, which is a path-traversal vulnerability, not a cosmetic naming issue.

The safe fix for path traversal is not just stripping `../` — it is to stop using client input in the physical path at all: reduce it to `path.basename()` at minimum, or better, generate the on-disk filename from a server-side UUID and keep the client's original filename only as DB metadata for display and download.

`file.mimetype` in Multer is populated verbatim from the `Content-Type` header of the multipart part, a value the client sets and fully controls — it is not derived from inspecting the file's actual bytes, so an allow-list check against it can be trivially bypassed by relabeling any file with an allowed Content-Type.

An extension- or declared-type allow-list is a reasonable first filter but is not sufficient on its own for production; it needs a magic-byte / content-sniffing layer (e.g. reading the leading bytes with a library like `file-type`) added on top of it, since a renamed executable sent with a spoofed `image/jpeg` header will otherwise pass untouched.

Using `Date.now()` alone as the uniqueness component of a generated filename only guarantees millisecond resolution — two requests arriving in the same millisecond, or two application instances behind a load balancer generating filenames independently, can produce an identical filename and silently overwrite one upload with another with no error raised.

When `diskStorage` writes the uploaded file to disk before any application-level validation (such as checking image dimensions) runs, a rejection at that later validation step leaves the already-written file orphaned on disk; the rejection path must explicitly delete the file (e.g. `fs.promises.unlink(file.path)`) or storage will slowly fill with rejected uploads over time.

In a code review, security-relevant defects like path traversal and spoofable content-type trust are blockers that should gate approval outright, while correctness and hygiene issues like filename collisions and orphaned files are must-fix-before-merge items — distinguishing the two categories, and pairing each finding with a concrete required fix rather than a vague call to "harden this," is itself part of reviewing well.

Verifying these fixes requires concrete evidence rather than trusting the fix on faith: a test uploading a filename containing traversal segments that must not land outside the upload directory, a test with a mislabeled binary payload that must be rejected, a concurrency test proving two same-instant uploads don't collide, and a test asserting no file remains on disk after a failed validation step.
